claim: Angioblasts are initially specified in the lateral plate mesoderm and migrate between the somites towards the midline, where they coalesce and assemble the dorsal aorta (DA) and the cardinal vein (CV) underneath the notochord (NC).
source: Angioblasts are initially specified in the lateral plate mesoderm and migrate between the somites towards the midline, where they coalesce and assemble the DA and the CV underneath the notochord (NC)
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in developmental biology and is presented as background information in the manuscript.

claim: Vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) has been previously proposed to regulate angioblast migration to the midline.
source: It has been previously proposed that this process is regulated by Vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) (Coultas et al., 2005; Verma et al., 2010; Gore et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: vegfaa transcripts are expressed in the somites between 12 and 15 hours post fertilization (hpf) in zebrafish.
source: As previously published (Nicoli et al., 2008), expression analysis of vegfaa, the gene for the main VEGF-A ortholog in zebrafish, showed the presence of transcripts in the somites between 12 and 15 hr post fertilization (hpf)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and is consistent with the timing shown in Figure 1B-F.

claim: Vegfa ligand depletion (vegfaa/vegfab MO) does not interfere with angioblast migration in zebrafish embryos.
source: Surprisingly, neither Vegfa ligand depletion (vegfaa/vegfab MO) nor a null mutation in the gene encoding the VEGFR2 ortholog (kdrl) interfered with angioblast migration in zebrafish embryos (Figure 1H,J)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and morpholino knockdown experiments.

claim: A null mutation in the kdrl gene (encoding VEGFR2 ortholog) does not interfere with angioblast migration in zebrafish embryos.
source: Surprisingly, neither Vegfa ligand depletion (vegfaa/vegfab MO) nor a null mutation in the gene encoding the VEGFR2 ortholog (kdrl) interfered with angioblast migration in zebrafish embryos (Figure 1H,J)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic mutant analysis shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Vegfa signaling dependent phenotypes, like failure to form the intersegmental vessels, can be observed after 24 hpf in Vegfa-deficient embryos.
source: although Vegfa signaling dependent phenotypes, like failure to form the intersegmental vessels, could be observed after 24 hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, demonstrating that the Vegfa knockdown was effective.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Vegfr2 signaling from 6 to 17 hpf does not impair angioblast migration to the midline.
source: Additionally, pharmacological inhibition of Vegfr2 signaling from 6 to 17 hpf did not impair angioblast migration to the midline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using chemical inhibitor treatment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Angioblast migration is not affected after Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) inhibition using cyclopamine.
source: In line with our previous experiments, angioblast migration was not affected after Shh inhibition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using cyclopamine treatment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vegfa signaling is dispensable for angioblast specification or migration in zebrafish.
source: The sum of these data strongly indicates that Vegfa signaling is dispensable for angioblast specification or migration in zebrafish.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from multiple experimental results including morpholino knockdown, genetic mutants, and pharmacological inhibition.

claim: Apelin receptor a (aplnra) is expressed in migrating angioblasts.
source: As previously published (Scott et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2007), we detected expression of apelin receptor a (aplnra) and apelin receptor b (aplnrb) in migrating angioblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B and citations to prior work.

claim: Apelin receptor b (aplnrb) is expressed in migrating angioblasts.
source: As previously published (Scott et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2007), we detected expression of apelin receptor a (aplnra) and apelin receptor b (aplnrb) in migrating angioblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B and citations to prior work.

claim: MO-mediated knockdown of apelin receptor a or b partially inhibits midline migration of angioblasts.
source: MO-mediated knockdown of apelin receptor a or b partially inhibited midline migration, while simultaneous loss of both apelin receptor genes completely abolished midline migration of angioblasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Simultaneous loss of both apelin receptor genes (aplnra and aplnrb) completely abolishes midline migration of angioblasts.
source: MO-mediated knockdown of apelin receptor a or b partially inhibited midline migration, while simultaneous loss of both apelin receptor genes completely abolished midline migration of angioblasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from double morpholino knockdown shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Embryos with homozygous mutations in the ligand ela display impaired migration of angioblasts.
source: Likewise, embryos with homozygous mutations in the ligand ela display impaired migration of angioblasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ela mutant analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mutations in apln receptor genes show an additive effect on angioblast migration phenotype severity.
source: Genotyping of individual embryos revealed an additive effect, while mild phenotypes were observed when one receptor gene was homozygously mutant, phenotypic strength increased with additional loss of functional receptor genes
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic analysis data shown in Figure 2B,C correlating genotype with phenotype.

claim: Apelin (Apln) deficiency can partially be compensated by Elabela (Ela).
source: Ela deficiency can partially be compensated by Apln.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic analysis of apln/ela double mutants shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Homozygous ela−/−; apln−/− double mutants phenocopy apln receptor deficiency.
source: ela−/−; apln double mutants phenocopied apln receptor deficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing double mutants to receptor mutants shown in Figure 2A,B,E.

claim: MO-mediated knockdown of apln shows no difference to control MO injected embryos in angioblast migration.
source: Next, we analyzed the requirement for the ligand Apln by MO-mediated gene knockdown and, unexpectedly, observed no difference to control MO injected embryos (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from morpholino knockdown shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Homozygous aplnmu267 mutant embryos show no vasculogenesis defects.
source: Consistent with the MO-mediated depletion, homozygous aplnmu267 mutant embryos (Figure 2A) showed no vasculogenesis defects
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic mutant analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Endogenous Apln is not sufficient to regulate angioblast migration to the midline.
source: which indicated that endogenous Apln is not sufficient to regulate angioblast migration to the midline
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the lack of phenotype in apln mutants and morphants.

claim: Apln receptors are required in myocardial development in zebrafish.
source: Previous studies have identified a requirement for Apln receptors in myocardial development in zebrafish (Scott et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2007) and mice (Charo et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Apln receptors are required in myocardial development in mice.
source: Previous studies have identified a requirement for Apln receptors in myocardial development in zebrafish (Scott et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2007) and mice (Charo et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Apln deficiency could not completely phenocopy Apln receptor deficiency in myocardial development.
source: which could not completely be phenocopied by Apln deficiency (Scott et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2007; Charo et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Elabela (Ela) is a novel peptide hormone that binds and activates Apln receptors.
source: Recently, a novel peptide hormone named Elabela (Ela, also known as Apela or Toddler) was identified in zebrafish and shown to bind and activate Aplnrs (Chng et al., 2013; Pauli et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: ela is expressed by the notochord.
source: By in situ hybridization we detected ela expression by the NC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, [Pauli et al., 2014])
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and citation to prior work.

claim: Ela-Aplnr represent a novel bona fide ligand–receptor pair regulating angioblast migration.
source: indicating that indeed Ela-Aplnr represent a novel bona fide ligand–receptor pair and therefore a novel signaling pathway regulating angioblast migration
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the ela mutant phenotype and receptor expression data.

claim: ela expression increases later in the notochord while apln expression becomes progressively reduced.
source: Given that the ela-/- phenotype was not as severe as the depletion of both receptors and that apln expression increases later in the NC (while ela expression becomes progressively reduced, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing temporal expression patterns in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: A mild angioblast migration phenotype is observed when either one ela allele or both apln alleles are mutant.
source: Interestingly a mild phenotype was observed, when either one ela or both apln alleles were mutant
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic analysis data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: A strong angioblast migration phenotype is observed when ela is homozygously mutant.
source: a strong phenotype when ela was homozygously mutant with increasing severity (severe phenotype) upon loss of the apln alleles
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic analysis data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Phenotype severity increases upon loss of apln alleles in ela mutant embryos.
source: a strong phenotype when ela was homozygously mutant with increasing severity (severe phenotype) upon loss of the apln alleles
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic analysis data showing dose dependency in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Ela and Apln act as chemoattractants for angioblast migration to the midline.
source: The observed dose dependency is indicative, that in this context Ela and Apln might act as novel chemoattractants for angioblast migration to the midline
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the dose-dependent genetic data.

claim: Ela acts as the major endogenous attractant for angioblast migration.
source: with Ela acting as the major endogenous attractant and Apln having a minor additive role
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the relative severity of phenotypes in ela vs apln mutants.

claim: Apln has a minor additive role in angioblast migration.
source: with Ela acting as the major endogenous attractant and Apln having a minor additive role
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the genetic analysis showing additive effects.

claim: Signals from the midline guide angioblast migration in zebrafish embryos lacking the notochord.
source: Previous analysis of zebrafish embryos lacking the NC showed, that signals from the midline guide angioblast migration
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and is consistent with data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Angioblasts fail to migrate to the midline position in notochord mutants noto and ta.
source: Angioblasts fail to migrate to the midline position in the NC mutants noto and ta.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Notochord deficiency abolishes or strongly reduces ela expression in noto or ta mutant embryos.
source: NC deficiency abolishes or strongly reduces ela expression in noto or ta mutant embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mosaic expression of Ela in the midline rescues angioblast migration in ta mutant embryos.
source: Mosaic expression of Ela in the midline, achieved by injection of shh:ela DNA, led to rescue of angioblast migration in ta mutant embryos (n = 61 embryos, ctr injected n = 32 embryos). Significance was calculated by chi-square (χb1602 = 19.65) equivalent to p < 0.001 (p = 9E-06).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental rescue data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ela expression is sufficient to guide angioblasts to the midline.
source: ela expression is sufficient to guide angioblasts to the midline.
evidence: This claim is supported by the rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3 and ectopic expression experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Ela does not act as a chemoattractant but instead acts as a motogen in regulating mesoderm migration during gastrulation.
source: Recently, it was published that Ela does not act as a chemoattractant, but instead acts as a motogen in regulating mesoderm migration during gastrulation
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Significantly more Ela overexpressing cells attract angioblasts than control cells in noto mutant embryos.
source: Quantification of Ela/RFP or ctr (Cherry) positive cells showed significantly more Ela overexpressing cells attracting angioblasts than ctr cells (n = 10 embryos for hs:ela, n = 20 embryos for hs:ctr ; p*** = 0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Significantly more Ela overexpressing cells attract angioblasts than control cells in ta mutant embryos.
source: Quantification of Ela/RFP or ctr (Cherry) positive cells showed significantly more Ela overexpressing cells attracting angioblasts than ctr cells (n = 8 embryos for hs:ela, n = 10 embryos for hs:ctr ; p** = 0.0089).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Ela acts as a chemoattractant for angioblasts during vasculogenesis.
source: Quantification of Ela/RFP or ctr (Cherry) positive cells showed significantly more Ela overexpressing cells attracting angioblasts than ctr cells
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ectopic expression experiments showing that angioblasts are attracted to cells expressing Ela, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: 93.6% of control MO injected donor angioblasts migrated to the midline in wild type host embryos.
source: 93.6% of ctr MO injected (n = 39 GFP + angioblasts, 7 embryos), but only 9.4% of aplnra/b deficient (aplnra/b MO injected; n = 62 GFP+ angioblasts, 5 embryos) donor angioblasts migrated to the midline in WT host embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative transplantation experiment data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Only 9.4% of aplnra/b deficient donor angioblasts migrated to the midline in wild type host embryos.
source: 93.6% of ctr MO injected (n = 39 GFP + angioblasts, 7 embryos), but only 9.4% of aplnra/b deficient (aplnra/b MO injected; n = 62 GFP+ angioblasts, 5 embryos) donor angioblasts migrated to the midline in WT host embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative transplantation experiment data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 81.9% of wild type donor angioblasts migrated to the midline in aplnra/b deficient host embryos.
source: In contrast, 81.9% of WT donor angioblasts (n = 15 GFP+ angioblasts, 6 embryos) migrated to the midline in aplnra/b deficient host embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative transplantation experiment data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ela-Aplnr signaling is directly required in angioblasts for their migration to the midline.
source: To prove that Ela-Aplnr signaling is directly required in angioblasts and rule out that the observed migration defects were caused by changes in other cell types, we performed transplantation experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by transplantation experiment data showing cell-autonomous requirement, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ela expression at the embryonic midline provides a chemoattractive signal for Aplnr-positive angioblasts.
source: Based on the sum of the results presented above, we propose that Ela expression at the embryonic midline provides a chemoattractive signal for Aplnr-positive angioblasts.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the combined results of expression analysis, mutant analysis, rescue experiments, and transplantation experiments.

claim: Initial ela expression at the midline appears stronger than apln expression.
source: While Ela and Apln both signal to the Apln receptors, the initial ela expression at the midline appears stronger than apln, which peaked at later developmental time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data comparing expression patterns shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: apln expression peaks at later developmental time points than ela.
source: While Ela and Apln both signal to the Apln receptors, the initial ela expression at the midline appears stronger than apln, which peaked at later developmental time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing temporal expression patterns in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: ela and apln may have partially redundant functions but are required at different stages of vascular morphogenesis.
source: Thus, ela and apln may have partially redundant functions, but are required at different stages of vascular morphogenesis.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the temporal expression patterns and genetic interaction data.

claim: Ela-Aplnr signaling was strictly required for the guided migration of angioblasts.
source: Surprisingly, while Ela-Aplnr signaling was strictly required for the guided migration of angioblasts, this process was not controlled by Vegfa-mediated signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data from receptor mutants, ligand mutants, and transplantation experiments.

claim: Angioblast migration is not controlled by Vegfa-mediated signaling.
source: Surprisingly, while Ela-Aplnr signaling was strictly required for the guided migration of angioblasts, this process was not controlled by Vegfa-mediated signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing normal migration in Vegfa-deficient embryos.

claim: Ela-Aplnr signaling represents a novel signaling pathway for angioblasts regulating vascular patterning in the developing vertebrate embryo.
source: Our studies identified Ela-Aplnr signaling as a novel signaling pathway for angioblasts regulating vascular patterning in the developing vertebrate embryo.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the combined experimental results demonstrating a previously unknown role for this pathway.

claim: The Ela-Aplnr signaling pathway may represent a novel therapeutic target in human disease.
source: As therapeutic intervention with vascular growth is clinically highly relevant and, so far, predominantly focuses on the VEGF-A signaling cascade, the Ela-Aplnr signaling pathway may also represent a novel therapeutic target in human disease.
evidence: This claim is speculative, extrapolating from the zebrafish findings to potential clinical applications.

claim: Global inactivation of genes encoding VEGF-A or VEGFR2 in mice led to strong vascular defects affecting the whole vascular network including the dorsal aorta.
source: Global inactivation of the genes encoding VEGF-A or the corresponding receptor VEGFR2 in mice led to strong vascular defects affecting the whole vascular network including the DA (Shalaby et al., 1995; Ferrara et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work in mice.

claim: In Xenopus embryos, vegfa transcripts are expressed in the midline.
source: In Xenopus embryos, transcripts for the vegfa gene are expressed in the midline and migrating angioblasts were guided towards sites of ectopic Vegfa expression (Cleaver and Krieg, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work in Xenopus.

claim: In Xenopus embryos, migrating angioblasts were guided towards sites of ectopic Vegfa expression.
source: In Xenopus embryos, transcripts for the vegfa gene are expressed in the midline and migrating angioblasts were guided towards sites of ectopic Vegfa expression (Cleaver and Krieg, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work in Xenopus.

claim: Activity of Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) in the midline induces vegfaa expression.
source: As activity of Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) in the midline has been shown to induce vegfaa expression (Lawson et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: vegfaa expression in the somites is abolished in embryos treated with Cyclopamine.
source: vegfaa expression in the somites is abolished in embryos treated with 100 μM Cyclopamine (CyA) from 11 hpf to 18 hpf.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Embryos treated with Cyclopamine from 11 hpf to 18 hpf to block Sonic hedgehog signaling showed no defects in medial angioblast migration.
source: Embryos treated with 100 μM Cyclopamine (CyA) from 11 hpf to 18 hpf to block Sonic hedgehog signaling showed no defects in medial angioblast migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: At 17 hpf, angioblasts in control embryos as well as Vegfa signaling deficient embryos arrived at the midline.
source: At 17 hpf, angioblasts in control embryos as well as Vegfa signaling deficient embryos arrived at the midline (A, B, C, G, H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Control embryos showed sprouting of the intersegmental vessels while Vegfa signaling deficient embryos lacked the intersegmental vessels.
source: Control embryos showed sprouting of the intersegmental vessels (D, F, K) whereas Vegfa signaling deficient embryos lacked the intersegmental vessels (E, J, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: aplnra is expressed in the paraxial mesoderm at 12 hpf.
source: aplnra expression is strong in the paraxial mesoderm (A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: aplnrb is strongly expressed in the angioblasts prior to migration at 12 hpf.
source: At 12 hpf, aplnrb is strongly expressed in the angioblasts (prior to migration, arrowheads) and within the lateral plate mesoderm and at the notochord somite boundary.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both aplnra and aplnrb receptors are expressed in the angioblasts at 18 hpf.
source: Both receptors are expressed in the angioblasts at 18 hpf (A, B, arrowheads)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Both aplnra and aplnrb receptors are expressed in the developing axial vessels at 20 hpf.
source: and in the developing axial vessels at 20 hpf (Arrowheads point to the DA, arrows to the PCV).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Prior to angioblast migration, both apln and ela are expressed by the notochord.
source: Prior to angioblast migration apln and ela are both expressed by the notochord, with ela showing a much stronger expression (C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: ela shows much stronger expression than apln in the notochord prior to angioblast migration.
source: Prior to angioblast migration apln and ela are both expressed by the notochord, with ela showing a much stronger expression (C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: After angioblasts reached the midline (18 hpf, 20 hpf), only apln is still expressed by the notochord.
source: After angioblasts reached the midline (18 hpf, 20 hpf) only apln is still expressed by the notochord, whereas notochord derived ela expression is strongly reduced to absent.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Notochord derived ela expression is strongly reduced to absent after angioblasts reached the midline (18 hpf, 20 hpf).
source: After angioblasts reached the midline (18 hpf, 20 hpf) only apln is still expressed by the notochord, whereas notochord derived ela expression is strongly reduced to absent.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Knockdown of aplnr does not influence the specification of angioblasts.
source: Knockdown of aplnr does not influence the specification of angioblasts. In situ hybridizations detecting expression of the angioblast marker etv2 at 13.5 hpf (dorsal views).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data for etv2 expression shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: An 8 base pair insertion in aplnra leads to a premature stop and a shortening of the Aplnra protein to 13 amino acids.
source: An 8 base pair insertion, shown as lower case letters in blue leads to a premature stop and a shortening of the Aplnra protein to 13 AA.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A 4 base pair insertion in aplnrb leads to a premature stop and a shortening of the Aplnrb protein to 65 amino acids.
source: A 4 base pair insertion, shown as lower case letters in blue leads to a premature stop and a shortening of the Aplnrb protein to 65 AA.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A 1 base pair loss / 9 base pair insertion in apln causes a frameshift leading to a premature stop codon and a shortening of the Apln protein to 11 amino acids.
source: An 1 baise pair loss / 9 base pair insertion, shown as lower case letters in blue causes a frameshift leading to a premature stop codon and a shortening of the Apln protein to 11 AA.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Angioblasts migrate towards the midline and coalesce underneath the notochord to form the first axial vessels.
source: A key step in the de novo formation of the embryonic vasculature is the migration of endothelial precursors, the angioblasts, to the position of the future vessels. To form the first axial vessels, angioblasts migrate towards the midline and coalesce underneath the notochord.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and is visualized in Figure 1.

claim: Angioblasts rely on their intrinsic expression of Apelin receptors (Aplr, APJ) for their migration to the midline.
source: Here we challenge this model and instead demonstrate that angioblasts rely on their intrinsic expression of Apelin receptors (Aplr, APJ) for their migration to the midline.
evidence: This claim is supported by transplantation experiments and receptor expression data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: During angioblast migration, Apelin receptor signaling is mainly triggered by the ligand Elabela (Ela).
source: We further show that during this angioblast migration Apelin receptor signaling is mainly triggered by the recently discovered ligand Elabela (Ela).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic analysis showing ela has a stronger phenotype than apln, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Neither Ela, Apelin, nor their receptors have previously been implicated in regulating angioblast migration.
source: As neither of the ligands Ela or Apelin (Apln) nor their receptors have previously been implicated in regulating angioblast migration, we hereby provide a novel mechanism for regulating vasculogenesis
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of prior literature on this topic, as indicated by the novelty of the findings.

claim: The Ela-Aplnr mechanism for regulating vasculogenesis has direct relevance to physiological and pathological angiogenesis.
source: we hereby provide a novel mechanism for regulating vasculogenesis, with direct relevance to physiological and pathological angiogenesis.
evidence: This claim is speculative, extrapolating from the developmental findings to broader biological contexts.
